Hotter-than-expected US inflation raises prospect of a larger December Fed hike: Following the release of October CPI, which showed both headline and core inflation rising more than expected, markets have moved to fully price in a 25-basis-point rate hike at next month's FOMC meeting. The question now is whether traders will begin positioning for a larger 50-basis-point move following Fed Governor Waller's hawkish comments earlier today.

The repricing has triggered a sharp bear flattening of the US Treasury yield curve, with the policy-sensitive two-year yield rising 11.5 basis points compared with a 5-basis-point increase in the ten-year yield, narrowing the 2s10s spread by 6.5 basis points. The move highlights growing concerns that persistent inflation will force the Fed to maintain a restrictive policy stance for longer, potentially at the expense of economic growth. Meanwhile, the sharp rise in December 2027 SOFR-implied rates relative to December 2026 suggests markets are also reassessing the longer-term policy outlook, with fewer rate cuts, or potentially additional tightening, being priced beyond next year.

However, the risk for those betting on further tightening, especially a larger 50-basis-point hike, is that inflation pressures may already be easing. While the November CPI report will not be released until after the December FOMC meeting, signs of moderating price pressures - through lower energy prices - in the intervening weeks could put a spanner in the works of an increasingly hawkish market. Such a development would leave the Fed facing a difficult balancing act between responding to backward-looking inflation data and avoiding excessive tightening just as underlying price pressures begin to subside.

China’s record trade surplus raises fresh concerns over global trade imbalances

China’s year-to-date trade surplus reached a record USD 1.04 trillion in October, surpassing USD 958 billion during the same period last year and USD 790 billion in 2024. The widening imbalance highlights the continued strength of China’s export sector, even as domestic demand remains relatively subdued, reinforcing concerns that excess industrial capacity is increasingly being directed towards overseas markets.

During the first ten months of the year, China’s trade surplus with the EU reached a record USD 310 billion, already exceeding the USD 292 billion recorded for the whole of last year. Meanwhile, surpluses with Southeast Asia and the US climbed to USD 293 billion and USD 266.5 billion, respectively, up around 34% and 14% year on year.

October nevertheless brought some narrowing of the monthly surplus to USD 105.3 billion, below expectations, as imports surged partly driven by stronger purchases of crude oil, in dollar terms the strongest since 2022, and refined petroleum products, with both recording their biggest increase since March.
